---
title: "`Option`, `Result`, and the `?` Operator"
description: "One key Rust idea, one tiny executable example, the reason it works, and a precise pitfall."
---

## The question

**How does Rust force the caller to acknowledge a missing value or a recoverable error?**

Use `Option<T>` for `Some(T)` or `None`, and `Result<T,E>` for `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)`. The `?` operator propagates an error early to the caller.

## The core rule

Encode failure in the return type, instead of assuming every conversion works.

## One complete example

Paste these lines into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`, or [use the tested Rust examples project](examples/index.qmd).

~~~rust
fn double(s: &str) -> Result<i32, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    let n: i32 = s.parse()?; // Err returns early
    Ok(n * 2)
}
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", double("21")); // Ok(42)
    println!("{:?}", double("x"));  // Err(...)
}
~~~

**Walk through it:** The successful parse of `"21"` produces 21, then `Ok(42)`. Parsing `"x"` fails; `?` returns that error without executing the multiplication.

## Common misunderstanding

`unwrap()` panics on `Err`/`None`; use it only when failure truly violates a known invariant. For expected input errors, propagate `Result` or handle them with `match`.

## Remember it in one sentence

Encode failure in the return type, instead of assuming every conversion works.

**Official reference:** [The Rust Programming Language / Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html).
